# How to use this guide

Community Pharmacy and Management (ER20-22T) is a 75-hour second-year D.Pharm subject. It is a practice subject: most answers are about **what the pharmacist does, in what order, and why**. Learn the steps, tables and mnemonics, and practise saying the counselling points aloud as if a patient were in front of you.

The official syllabus numbers its chapters 1 to 7, then 9 and 10 (there is no chapter 8 in the PCI document). In this guide two pairs of small chapters are joined and the two largest chapters are split:

| Guide unit | Syllabus chapter | Hours in syllabus |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Community pharmacy practice, responsibilities, GPP and SOPs | 1 and 2 | 2 + 3 |
| 2. Prescription and prescription handling | 3 | 7 |
| 3. Communication skills | 4 | 6 |
| 4. Patient counselling | 5 | 10 |
| 5. Medication adherence and health screening | 6 and 7 | 2 + 5 |
| 6. OTC medications, self-medication, responding to symptoms | 9 (first half) | 15 (shared) |
| 7. Minor ailments and self-care advice | 9 (second half) | |
| 8. Setting up a pharmacy, purchasing and inventory control | 10 (first half) | 25 (shared) |
| 9. Finance, accounts, software, CRM, audits, SOPs, digital health | 10 (second half) | |

Chapters 9 and 10 together carry 40 of the 75 hours, so Units 6–9 deserve more than half of your study time.

## Exam pattern (ER-2020 theory paper)

D.Pharm ER-2020 exams are yearly and are conducted by the state examining board (for example HPTSB in Himachal Pradesh) under the PCI ER-2020 regulations. The theory paper is **80 marks, 3 hours**; another 20 marks come from sessional (internal) assessment. The usual ER-2020 paper looks like this. Confirm the pattern with your college, because boards sometimes change the format.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | Objective questions (MCQs / one-word / fill in the blanks) – all compulsory | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| II | Short answers – attempt 10 of 11 | 10 × 3 = 30 |
| III | Long answers – attempt 6 of 7 | 6 × 5 = 30 |

In this guide **long** questions are 5-mark answers and **short** questions are 3-mark answers, to match this pattern. A few **very-short** (2-mark) questions are added for quick revision and sessional tests.

## Probability ratings

- **High** – asked in most years or a core topic of the chapter; prepare the full answer.
- **Medium** – asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** – rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

The ratings are an estimate from the syllabus hours and the kind of questions usually set in D.Pharm papers. They are not a promise.

## Scoring tips for this subject

1. **Begin with a definition.** Prescription, patient counselling, adherence, OTC, self-medication, GPP, SOP, CRM, audit, inventory control – one or two clean lines first.
2. **Write steps as a numbered flow.** Prescription handling, dispensing process, stages of counselling, responding to symptoms and ordering stock are all step answers. A small ```text flow chart (A → B → C) earns marks.
3. **Use tables** for parts of a prescription, Latin abbreviations, ancillary labels, barriers and their remedies, WHO adherence factors, OTC categories, ABC/VED/FSN, licences, and types of audit.
4. **Learn the mnemonics:** WWHAM, ASMETHOD, SOLER, RICE, FEFO, and the three prime questions of counselling.
5. **Quote Indian law correctly:** Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 and Rules 1945; Pharmacy Act 1948; retail licences in Form 20 and Form 21; at least 10 m² retail area; Schedule H1 register kept 3 years; Schedule X prescription copy kept 2 years; Pharmacy Practice Regulations 2015; DPCO 2013. Do not guess fees or form numbers you are not sure of.
6. **For counselling questions** (hypertension, diabetes, asthma, TB, COPD, AIDS), write under headings: disease, medicines and how to take them, side effects, monitoring, lifestyle, danger signs.
7. **For minor ailment questions**, always write four parts: self-care advice, OTC products, counselling, and **when to refer**. Examiners look for referral points.
8. **For a 5-mark long answer**, aim for about one and a half pages: definition, flow chart or table, 5–6 explained points, a short conclusion. **For a 3-mark short answer**, 5–6 crisp points or a small table.
9. **Use your practical work.** Blood pressure measurement, glucometer use, inhaler technique, label writing and prescription checking are asked in theory too; the practical guides in this pack describe them step by step.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you have only a few hours, learn these with full points: **parts of a prescription and prescription handling**, **labelling and ancillary labels**, **dispensing errors**, **stages and barriers of counselling**, **counselling points for chronic diseases**, **adherence factors and strategies**, **health screening values**, **OTC and self-medication**, **minor ailments with referral points**, **legal requirements to open a pharmacy**, **inventory control (ABC, VED, EOQ)** and **day book and cash book**.

## Unit 1: Practice, responsibilities, GPP, SOPs

| Fact | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| Community pharmacy | Pharmacy serving the public directly – medicines plus advice |
| Pharmaceutical care concept | Hepler and Strand, 1990 |
| Pharmacy Act / Drugs and Cosmetics Act / Rules | 1948 / 1940 / 1945 |
| Pharmacy Practice Regulations | PCI, 2015 |
| GPP | FIP 1993; joint FIP/WHO guidelines 2011; four roles: supply, therapy management, professional performance, public health |
| SOP | Written, approved step-by-step instruction; parts – purpose, scope, responsibility, procedure, records, approval, review date |

## Unit 2: Prescription

- Parts: prescriber details, date, patient details, **Rx (superscription)**, **inscription** (drug, strength), **subscription** (to pharmacist), **signa** (to patient), refill, signature.
- Abbreviations: od, bd, tds, qid, hs, ac, pc, stat, sos, prn.
- Handling: receive → legality → completeness → clinical check → clarify → prepare → label → final check → counsel → record.
- Label: pharmacy, patient, drug + strength, directions, quantity, date, prescriber, "keep out of reach of children".
- Ancillary: shake well; external use only; may cause drowsiness; avoid alcohol; with food; swallow whole; complete course; refrigerate 2–8 °C.
- Errors: wrong drug (LASA), strength, form, dose, quantity, patient; prevent by tall-man lettering, separate storage, double check, counselling, error reporting.

| Schedule | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| H | Prescription only; Rx on label |
| H1 | Separate register, kept 3 years |
| X | Duplicate prescription, copy kept 2 years, lock and key |

## Unit 3: Communication

- Process: sender → message → channel → receiver → feedback; noise.
- Types: verbal, non-verbal, written, visual, electronic.
- SOLER: Square, Open, Lean, Eye contact, Relaxed. SBAR for talking to doctors.
- Questions: open, closed, probing, reflective; avoid leading.
- WWHAM: Who, What symptoms, How long, Action taken, Medicines.
- ASMETHOD: Age, Self, Medication, Extra medicines, Time, History, Other symptoms, Danger symptoms.

## Unit 4: Counselling

- Stages: introduction → content → process → closing (summary, teach-back, follow-up, document).
- Prime questions: what is it for, how to take it, what to expect.
- Barriers: patient (language, literacy, hearing), pharmacist (time, knowledge), environment (noise, privacy), system.

| Disease | Must-say points |
| --- | --- |
| Hypertension | Daily lifelong; less salt; exercise; do not stop suddenly; avoid NSAIDs/decongestants |
| Diabetes | Hypoglycaemia signs and 15–20 g sugar; insulin at 2–8 °C, rotate sites; foot care; HbA1c |
| Asthma | Reliever vs preventer; inhaler technique; rinse mouth after steroid; action plan |
| TB | Full 6-month course; orange urine (rifampicin); report jaundice; contraceptive interaction |
| COPD | Stop smoking; inhalers; vaccination; early care for flare-ups |
| AIDS | Very high ART adherence; interactions; safe sex; prophylaxis |

- PPI: manufacturer's patient leaflet in pack – required in EU, some products in USA (Medication Guides); not generally in India.
- PIL: simple leaflet on disease/medicine, often made by the pharmacist.

## Unit 5: Adherence and screening

- Adherence (WHO 2003); compliance is the older term; concordance = shared agreement.
- WHO factors: social/economic, health system, condition, therapy, patient.
- Fixes: counsel, simplify, FDCs, reminders, pill boxes, generics, family, DOT, follow-up.

| Screen | Refer at |
| --- | --- |
| BP | ≥140/90 mmHg repeated |
| Fasting glucose | ≥126 mg/dL (100–125 prediabetes) |
| Random glucose | ≥200 mg/dL |
| HbA1c | ≥6.5% |
| BMI (Asian) | 23–24.9 overweight; ≥25 obese |
| Waist | Men ≥90 cm, women ≥80 cm |
| SpO2 | <95% attention; <90% urgent |
| Peak flow | <80% of best warning; <50% danger |

BMI = kg ÷ m². A pharmacy reading is a screen, not a diagnosis.

## Units 6–7: OTC and minor ailments

- India has no legal OTC schedule; prescription drugs = H, H1, X; Schedule K exemptions (household remedies).
- Pharmacist: assess → decide (advise/supply/refer) → select → counsel → safety net → record.

| Ailment | First-line | Refer if |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pain | Paracetamol; ibuprofen with food; RICE | Worst-ever headache, stiff neck, back pain with leg weakness |
| Cough | Dry – suppressant/demulcent; wet – expectorant | >2–3 weeks, blood, breathlessness |
| Cold | Fluids, steam, saline, antihistamine; decongestant drops ≤1 week | >10 days, ear/facial pain |
| Diarrhoea | ORS; zinc in children; loperamide adults | Blood, fever, dehydration |
| Constipation | Fibre, fluids, ispaghula, lactulose | Blood, weight loss, change of habit |
| Vomiting | ORS, small meals | Blood, >24–48 h, dehydration |
| Fever | Paracetamol, fluids, tepid sponge; no aspirin in children | >3 days, fits, non-fading rash |
| Sore throat | Gargles, lozenges | Breathing/swallowing difficulty, >1 week |
| Skin | Clotrimazole (fungal), permethrin 5% (scabies, treat contacts), benzoyl peroxide (acne) | Infection, widespread |
| Oral | Choline salicylate gel; chlorhexidine; dentist for toothache | Ulcer >3 weeks |

## Unit 8: Setting up and inventory

- Licences: Form 20 (other than C, C1, X), Form 21 (C, C1); wholesale 20B/21B; Schedule X separate.
- Conditions: registered pharmacist, ≥10 m² retail (≥15 m² retail + wholesale), refrigerator, records, display licence.
- Other: shop and establishment/trade licence, GST, NDPS if narcotics.
- Site: population, doctors nearby, competition, visibility, rent.
- Design: dispensing counter, counselling area, refrigerator, locked Schedule X cupboard, expired-goods area.
- Reorder level = daily use × lead time + safety stock. EOQ = √(2AO/H).
- ABC (value: A ≈ 10–20% items, 70–80% value), VED (vital/essential/desirable), FSN (fast/slow/non-moving); FEFO.

## Unit 9: Finance and management

- Fixed vs working capital; break-even sales = fixed costs ÷ gross margin ratio; DPCO 2013, NPPA.
- Day book = journal, book of original entry, date order; cash book: receipts Dr (left), payments Cr (right); single/double/triple column; petty cash.
- Software: billing, stock, expiry, accounts, H1 register, interactions.
- CRM: reminders, home delivery, loyalty, camps, complaints.
- Audit: financial, stock, regulatory, prescription, clinical, self-inspection; cycle – standard → measure → compare → change → re-audit.
- Digital health: ABDM, ABHA, Telemedicine Guidelines 2020; mHealth apps; e-pharmacy draft rules 2018 not finalised.

# Handling and reviewing prescriptions for legal compliance and completeness

**Aim:** To receive, read and review prescriptions with professional standards, checking each for legal compliance and completeness (minimum five prescriptions).

> Carried out in the model community pharmacy using simulated prescriptions. A teacher or classmate acts as the patient; your work is assessed on a structured checklist.

## Principle

A pharmacist must never dispense from a prescription that is unclear, incomplete or not legally valid. A prescription is valid when it is written by a registered medical practitioner (RMP), dentist or veterinarian, carries the prescriber's name, address and registration number, is signed and dated, names the patient, and states the drug, strength, dose and quantity clearly. Extra rules apply to Schedule H, H1 and X drugs under the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945.

## Requirements

Five or more simulated prescriptions (including some with deliberate faults), prescription checklist, drug reference book (for example National Formulary of India), Schedule H1 register format, rubber stamp of the model pharmacy, pen, practical record book.

## Procedure

1. Greet the "patient", take the prescription with both hands and confirm the patient's name and whether the medicine is for them.
2. Read the whole prescription once without stopping; then read it line by line.
3. **Legal check:** prescriber's name, qualification, registration number, address; signature; date; patient name, age, sex, address.
4. **Completeness check** for each drug: generic or brand name, dosage form, strength, dose, frequency, route, duration, total quantity.
5. **Schedule check:** identify any Schedule H, H1 or X drug and the extra requirements (H1 register entry, Schedule X duplicate copy).
6. **Clinical check:** dose suitable for age and weight; obvious interactions; duplicate drugs; allergy or pregnancy questions to ask.
7. Interpret all abbreviations (od, bd, tds, hs, ac, pc, sos, stat).
8. List every problem found and decide the action: dispense, contact prescriber (role play the phone call), or refuse with a polite explanation.
9. For scheduled drugs, show how the prescription is stamped with the pharmacy name and date of supply and how the H1 register is filled.
10. Record each prescription in the observation table.

## Observations

| No. | Prescriber details complete? | Signed and dated? | Patient details? | Drug details complete? | Scheduled drug | Problems found | Action taken |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Yes | Yes | Yes | Duration missing | – | Duration not stated | Phoned prescriber; 5 days confirmed and noted |
| 2 | Registration no. missing | Yes | Yes | Yes | H1 (antibiotic) | Not legally complete | Referred back to prescriber |
| 3 | | | | | | | |
| 4 | | | | | | | |
| 5 | | | | | | | |

Sample H1 register entry:

```text
Date | Patient name & address | Prescriber name & address | Drug & quantity | Signature
12/06 | Ram Kumar, Shimla       | Dr A. Sharma, City Clinic  | Cefixime 200 mg × 10 | ……
```

## Result

Five prescriptions were reviewed for legality and completeness; the faults found and the professional action for each were recorded.

## Precautions

1. Never guess an unclear word or dose; always confirm with the prescriber.
2. Do not alter a prescription yourself; record any change agreed by phone (who, what, when).
3. Be polite when refusing; explain the reason and advise the patient.
4. Keep the patient's information confidential.

## Viva questions

1. **What makes a prescription legally valid?** RMP's name, address, registration number, signature, date, patient details and clear drug details.
2. **What is the superscription?** The symbol Rx.
3. **What is the inscription?** The drug name, dosage form and strength.
4. **For how long is the H1 register kept?** Three years.
5. **How long is a Schedule X prescription copy kept?** Two years.
6. **Why is a scheduled-drug prescription stamped?** To show it has been dispensed so that it cannot be used again.
7. **What would you do with an unsigned prescription?** Not dispense; contact the prescriber.

# Identifying drug–drug interactions in prescriptions and follow-up action

**Aim:** To identify drug–drug interactions in given prescriptions and decide the follow-up action (minimum two prescriptions).

## Principle

A **drug–drug interaction** happens when one drug changes the effect of another. It may be:

- **Pharmacokinetic** – one drug changes the absorption, distribution, metabolism or excretion of another (for example rifampicin speeds up the breakdown of oral contraceptives; antacids reduce absorption of tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones).
- **Pharmacodynamic** – the two drugs add to or oppose each other's action (for example warfarin with aspirin increases bleeding; two sedatives increase drowsiness).

Interactions are graded as **major** (avoid or needs urgent action), **moderate** (monitor or adjust) and **minor**. The pharmacist identifies them, judges their importance and acts – by counselling, timing the doses apart, or contacting the prescriber.

## Requirements

Simulated prescriptions with interacting drugs, drug interaction reference (National Formulary of India, standard reference books or interaction-checking software), practical record book.

## Procedure

1. Read the prescription and list all drugs, including any OTC or herbal products the patient says they take.
2. Check each pair of drugs in the reference book or software.
3. Write the interacting pair, the mechanism and the likely result.
4. Grade the severity (major / moderate / minor).
5. Decide the action:
   - Minor – counsel only.
   - Separable by time – advise a gap (for example antacid and ciprofloxacin at least 2 hours apart).
   - Moderate – counsel and monitor; inform the prescriber if needed.
   - Major – contact the prescriber before dispensing; suggest an alternative.
6. Role-play the phone call to the prescriber using SBAR.
7. Record the interaction, action and outcome.

## Observations

| Rx | Interacting drugs | Mechanism | Possible effect | Severity | Action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Warfarin + aspirin | Pharmacodynamic; aspirin also affects platelets and stomach lining | Increased bleeding | Major | Contacted prescriber; paracetamol suggested for pain |
| 2 | Ciprofloxacin + aluminium–magnesium antacid | Chelation reduces absorption | Lower antibiotic effect | Moderate | Take ciprofloxacin at least 2 hours before the antacid |
| 3 | Rifampicin + oral contraceptive | Enzyme induction | Contraceptive failure | Major | Counsel to use another method; inform prescriber |

## Result

Interactions in the given prescriptions were identified, graded and the appropriate follow-up actions recorded.

## Precautions

1. Use an up-to-date reference; do not rely on memory.
2. Ask about OTC, herbal and home remedies too.
3. Do not alarm the patient; discuss serious problems with the prescriber first.
4. Record every intervention.

## Viva questions

1. **Define drug interaction.** A change in the effect of one drug caused by another drug, food or substance.
2. **Give an example of enzyme induction.** Rifampicin reducing the effect of oral contraceptives.
3. **Why should tetracycline not be taken with antacids?** Metal ions chelate it and reduce absorption.
4. **What do you do for a major interaction?** Contact the prescriber before dispensing.
5. **What is SBAR?** Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation – a structure for talking to prescribers.
practicals.title: Identifying drug–drug interactions in prescriptions and follow-up action

# Preparing dispensing labels and auxiliary labels

**Aim:** To prepare main dispensing labels and suitable auxiliary (ancillary) labels for prescribed medications (minimum five).

## Principle

The label is the patient's reminder at home of how to use the medicine. A **main label** carries the identity of the pharmacy, patient and medicine and clear directions. **Auxiliary labels** add important warnings such as "Shake well" or "May cause drowsiness". **Pictograms** help people who cannot read the language.

## Requirements

Simulated prescriptions, blank label sheets or label-printing software, set of auxiliary labels or pictograms, containers, pen, reference book.

## Procedure

1. Read the prescription and interpret the directions; convert abbreviations into plain words (for example "1 tab bd pc" → "Take ONE tablet TWICE a day AFTER food").
2. Write or print the main label with:
   - name and address of the pharmacy;
   - prescription number and date;
   - patient's name;
   - drug name, strength and dosage form;
   - directions in simple words (dose, frequency, timing, route, duration);
   - quantity;
   - prescriber's name;
   - "Keep out of reach of children".
3. Select the auxiliary labels needed for each drug from a reference.
4. Add pictograms where the patient has low literacy.
5. Fix labels straight on the container without covering the manufacturer's batch and expiry details.
6. Check the label against the prescription.
7. Explain the label to the "patient".

## Observations

| Drug (as prescribed) | Directions written on main label | Auxiliary labels |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Amoxicillin oral suspension 250 mg/5 ml, 5 ml tds × 5 days | Take 5 ml THREE times a day for 5 days | Shake well; complete the course; store as directed after mixing |
| Cetirizine 10 mg, 1 od hs | Take ONE tablet at BEDTIME | May cause drowsiness; avoid alcohol |
| Calamine lotion, apply bd | Apply on the affected skin TWICE a day | For external use only; shake well |
| Diclofenac 50 mg, 1 bd pc | Take ONE tablet TWICE a day AFTER food | Take with food; swallow whole |
| Insulin pen | Inject as directed by doctor | Store in refrigerator 2–8 °C; do not freeze |

## Result

Main and auxiliary labels were prepared for five prescribed medicines and checked against the prescriptions.

## Precautions

1. Use simple words; avoid Latin abbreviations on the label.
2. Write numbers clearly ("ONE", "5 ml").
3. Do not cover the batch number or expiry date.
4. Choose only relevant auxiliary labels; too many confuse patients.

## Viva questions

1. **List the contents of a main label.** Pharmacy, patient, drug and strength, directions, quantity, date, prescriber, "keep out of reach of children".
2. **Which auxiliary label is used for metronidazole?** Avoid alcohol.
3. **Why "Swallow whole" on enteric-coated tablets?** Crushing destroys the coating and its protection.
4. **What is a pictogram?** A standard picture showing how to take a medicine.
5. **Why "complete the course" for antibiotics?** To cure the infection and prevent resistance.
practicals.title: Preparing dispensing labels and auxiliary labels

# Blood pressure recording

**Aim:** To record the blood pressure of a subject with a sphygmomanometer and interpret the reading for monitoring or referral.

## Principle

**Blood pressure** is the pressure of blood on the walls of the arteries. **Systolic** pressure is the highest pressure when the heart contracts; **diastolic** pressure is the lowest pressure when the heart relaxes. It is written as systolic/diastolic in mmHg.

In the **auscultatory method**, a cuff on the upper arm is inflated to stop blood flow in the brachial artery and then slowly deflated. The first tapping sound heard with a stethoscope (Korotkoff sounds) marks the systolic pressure, and the point where the sounds disappear marks the diastolic pressure. **Digital (oscillometric) monitors** detect the vibrations of the artery wall and calculate the values automatically.

## Requirements

Validated digital BP monitor or aneroid sphygmomanometer with stethoscope, cuffs of correct sizes, chair with back support, table, record sheet.

## Procedure

1. Explain the test and get consent. Ask the subject to avoid smoking, caffeine and exercise for 30 minutes before.
2. Seat the subject comfortably with back supported, feet flat, legs uncrossed; rest for 5 minutes; no talking during measurement.
3. Bare the upper arm; support it on the table at heart level.
4. Choose the correct cuff size (bladder should cover most of the arm circumference). Wrap the cuff snugly with its lower edge about 2–3 cm above the elbow crease and the artery marker over the brachial artery.
5. **Digital:** press start and wait for the reading.
6. **Manual:** feel the radial pulse, inflate until it disappears and note the pressure; deflate. Place the stethoscope over the brachial artery, inflate to about 30 mmHg above that point, then deflate at 2–3 mmHg per second. Note the first sound (systolic) and the disappearance of sounds (diastolic).
7. Take a second reading after 1–2 minutes; record the average. Note pulse rate.
8. Record date, time, arm, position and readings; interpret and advise.

## Observations

| Reading | Systolic (mmHg) | Diastolic (mmHg) | Pulse (/min) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | | | |
| 2 | | | |
| Mean | | | |

**Interpretation (adults, office readings):**

| Category | Systolic | Diastolic |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Normal | Below 120 | Below 80 |
| Raised / high-normal | 120–139 | 80–89 |
| Hypertension | 140 or more | 90 or more |
| Very high – urgent referral | 180 or more | 110 or more |

## Result

The blood pressure of the subject was ……/…… mmHg (mean of two readings), which is classified as ………; advice/referral given: ………

## Precautions

1. Rest the subject for 5 minutes; arm at heart level; correct cuff size (a small cuff gives a falsely high reading).
2. Do not measure over clothing.
3. Deflate slowly in the manual method.
4. Use validated, calibrated equipment.
5. One raised reading is not a diagnosis – advise repeat readings or referral.

## Viva questions

1. **What is systolic pressure?** Highest arterial pressure during heart contraction.
2. **What are Korotkoff sounds?** Sounds heard over the artery as the cuff is deflated, used to find systolic and diastolic pressure.
3. **What BP is taken as hypertension in a pharmacy screen?** 140/90 mmHg or more on repeated readings.
4. **Effect of a small cuff?** Falsely high reading.
5. **Why rest before measuring?** Activity and anxiety raise BP.
practicals.title: Blood pressure recording

# Capillary blood glucose monitoring

**Aim:** To measure capillary blood glucose with a glucometer and interpret the result for monitoring or referral.

## Principle

A **glucometer** measures glucose in a small drop of capillary blood placed on a test strip. The strip contains an enzyme (glucose oxidase or glucose dehydrogenase) that reacts with glucose and produces an electric current proportional to the glucose concentration; the meter shows the value in mg/dL.

Values are interpreted according to the time since the last meal (fasting, after meals or random).

## Requirements

Glucometer, matching unexpired test strips, lancing device and sterile single-use lancets, 70% alcohol swabs, dry cotton, disposable gloves, sharps container, biomedical waste bin, record sheet. Control solution for checking the meter.

## Procedure

1. Explain the test, ask about the last meal, and get consent.
2. Wash your hands and wear gloves. Ask the subject to wash and dry hands (warm water improves blood flow).
3. Check the strip expiry and that the strip code (if any) matches the meter. Insert a strip; the meter switches on.
4. Clean the side of a fingertip (middle or ring finger) with alcohol and let it dry completely.
5. Prick the side of the fingertip with the lancing device.
6. Wipe away the first drop if advised by the meter maker; gently press to form a drop – do not squeeze hard.
7. Touch the drop to the strip's edge; let it fill.
8. Read and record the result; press dry cotton on the site.
9. Discard the lancet into the sharps container and the strip and cotton into the correct waste bin.
10. Interpret the result and advise.

## Observations

| Subject | Time since last meal | Reading (mg/dL) | Interpretation | Advice |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Fasting (8 h) | | | |
| 2 | Random | | | |

**Guide values:**

| Test | Normal | Prediabetes | Suggests diabetes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fasting | Below 100 | 100–125 | 126 or more |
| 2 hours after glucose / meal | Below 140 | 140–199 | 200 or more |
| Random with symptoms | – | – | 200 or more |

Below 70 mg/dL is low (hypoglycaemia) – give quick sugar and refer if needed.

## Result

The capillary blood glucose of the subject was ……… mg/dL (……… state), which is ………; advice given: ………

## Precautions

1. Use a new sterile lancet for every person; never share lancing devices.
2. Let alcohol dry before pricking (it can dilute the drop).
3. Use the side of the fingertip – less painful.
4. Do not squeeze hard (tissue fluid dilutes blood).
5. Store strips in their closed container; check expiry.
6. A meter reading is a screen – refer for laboratory confirmation.

## Viva questions

1. **Which enzyme is used on glucose strips?** Glucose oxidase or glucose dehydrogenase.
2. **Fasting glucose suggesting diabetes?** 126 mg/dL or more.
3. **Why use the side of the fingertip?** Fewer nerve endings, less pain.
4. **How are lancets disposed of?** In a puncture-proof sharps container as biomedical waste.
5. **What is hypoglycaemia?** Blood glucose below about 70 mg/dL with symptoms such as sweating and shaking.
practicals.title: Capillary blood glucose monitoring

# Lung function assessment with a peak flow meter and incentive spirometer

**Aim:** To measure peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) with a peak flow meter, and to demonstrate the use of an incentive spirometer.

## Principle

**Peak expiratory flow rate** is the fastest speed (litres per minute) at which a person can blow air out after a full breath in. It falls when the airways are narrowed, so it is used to monitor asthma and to follow an asthma action plan. Results are compared with the person's **personal best** or with a **predicted value** for age, sex and height.

An **incentive spirometer** encourages slow, deep breathing in. The patient breathes in through the mouthpiece and tries to raise a piston or ball to a target level. It is used after surgery and in lung disease to expand the lungs and prevent collapse of air sacs.

## Requirements

Peak flow meter with disposable mouthpieces, predicted-value chart, incentive spirometer, record sheet, tissues.

## Procedure

### Peak flow meter

1. Explain the test; fit a new mouthpiece; set the pointer to zero.
2. The subject stands (or sits upright) and holds the meter horizontally without blocking the pointer.
3. Take the deepest possible breath in.
4. Seal the lips tightly around the mouthpiece.
5. Blow out as hard and fast as possible in one short blast.
6. Note the reading; reset the pointer.
7. Repeat three times; record the **highest** of the three.
8. Compare with personal best or predicted value and find the zone.

### Incentive spirometer

1. Sit upright; hold the device upright at eye level.
2. Breathe out normally, then seal lips around the mouthpiece.
3. Breathe in slowly and deeply so that the indicator rises to the target; keep the flow indicator in the "best" range.
4. Hold the breath for 3–5 seconds, then breathe out slowly.
5. Rest a few seconds; repeat about 10 times as advised; cough to clear secretions.

## Observations

| Attempt | PEFR (L/min) |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | |
| 2 | |
| 3 | |
| Best | |

```text
% of predicted (or personal best) = Best PEFR ÷ predicted (or personal best) × 100
Zones: Green ≥80%  |  Yellow 50–80%  |  Red <50% (urgent care)
```

## Result

The best PEFR of the subject was ……… L/min, which is ………% of predicted, in the ……… zone. The use of the incentive spirometer was demonstrated.

## Precautions

1. Use a fresh mouthpiece for each person.
2. Fingers must not block the pointer; tongue must not block the mouthpiece.
3. Blow as fast as possible – it is a short blast, not a long blow.
4. Take the best of three readings.
5. With the incentive spirometer, breathe in slowly; stop if dizzy.

## Viva questions

1. **What is PEFR?** The fastest rate of air flow during a forced breath out.
2. **Unit of PEFR?** Litres per minute.
3. **Which reading is recorded?** The highest of three.
4. **What does the red zone mean?** Below 50% of best – severe narrowing, urgent medical care.
5. **Purpose of an incentive spirometer?** Encourages slow deep breaths to expand the lungs, e.g. after surgery.
practicals.title: Lung function assessment with a peak flow meter and incentive spirometer

# Recording capillary oxygen saturation with a pulse oximeter

**Aim:** To record the oxygen saturation (SpO2) and pulse rate of a subject with a fingertip pulse oximeter and interpret the result.

## Principle

Oxygenated and deoxygenated haemoglobin absorb red and infrared light differently. A **pulse oximeter** shines these two lights through the fingertip and measures how much passes through at each heartbeat. From the ratio, it calculates the percentage of haemoglobin carrying oxygen – the **peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2)** – and also shows the pulse rate.

## Requirements

Fingertip pulse oximeter with working batteries, alcohol swab, record sheet.

## Procedure

1. Explain the test and get consent.
2. Seat the subject and let them rest for a few minutes.
3. Remove nail polish or artificial nails from the finger used; warm cold hands.
4. Clean the oximeter's finger pad.
5. Place the oximeter on the index or middle finger, nail upwards; keep the hand still, resting at heart level.
6. Wait until the reading is steady (usually 30–60 seconds) and the pulse signal is strong.
7. Record SpO2 and pulse rate.
8. Interpret and advise.

## Observations

| Subject | SpO2 (%) | Pulse rate (/min) | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | | | |
| 2 | | | |

| SpO2 | Meaning (at rest, adults) |
| --- | --- |
| 95–100% | Normal |
| 91–94% | Low – needs medical advice |
| 90% or below | Very low – urgent medical care |

## Result

The SpO2 of the subject was ………% with a pulse rate of ……… per minute, which is ………

## Precautions

1. Remove nail polish; cold fingers and movement give false readings.
2. Wait for a stable reading.
3. Bright light on the sensor can affect the reading.
4. Readings may be less accurate with very poor circulation or darker skin pigmentation; consider the patient's symptoms too.
5. Breathlessness or chest pain needs referral whatever the reading.

## Viva questions

1. **What does SpO2 measure?** Percentage of haemoglobin saturated with oxygen in peripheral blood.
2. **Normal SpO2?** About 95–100%.
3. **Which lights are used?** Red and infrared.
4. **Why remove nail polish?** It blocks light and gives a false reading.
5. **When would you refer urgently?** SpO2 90% or below, or with breathlessness or chest pain.
practicals.title: Recording capillary oxygen saturation with a pulse oximeter

# BMI measurement

**Aim:** To measure the height and weight of a subject, calculate the Body Mass Index (BMI), measure waist circumference, and interpret the results.

## Principle

**Body Mass Index** relates weight to height and is used to screen for underweight, overweight and obesity:

```text
BMI (kg/m²) = Weight (kg) ÷ [Height (m)]²
```

Asian Indians develop diabetes and heart disease at lower BMI, so lower cut-offs are used in India. **Waist circumference** shows fat around the abdomen (central obesity), which is linked with diabetes and heart disease.

## Requirements

Calibrated weighing scale, stadiometer or wall-mounted height scale, non-stretch measuring tape, calculator or BMI chart, record sheet.

## Procedure

1. Explain the test and get consent.
2. **Weight:** check the scale reads zero; subject removes shoes and heavy items, stands still in the centre; record to the nearest 0.1 kg.
3. **Height:** subject removes shoes, stands with heels, buttocks, shoulders and back of head against the scale, looking straight ahead; lower the headpiece to touch the top of the head; record to the nearest 0.1 cm.
4. **Waist:** subject stands relaxed; place the tape horizontally midway between the lowest rib and the top of the hip bone; read at the end of a normal breath out.
5. Calculate BMI and classify; interpret waist circumference.
6. Give advice on diet and activity; refer where needed.

## Observations

| Parameter | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Weight (kg) | |
| Height (m) | |
| BMI (kg/m²) | |
| Waist circumference (cm) | |

**Worked example:** weight 68 kg, height 1.62 m → 1.62 × 1.62 = 2.62 → BMI = 68 ÷ 2.62 = 26.0 kg/m² → obese (Asian cut-off).

| BMI (Asian Indian adults) | Class |
| --- | --- |
| Below 18.5 | Underweight |
| 18.5–22.9 | Normal |
| 23–24.9 | Overweight |
| 25 or more | Obese |

Waist circumference: central obesity at 90 cm or more in men and 80 cm or more in women (Indian adults).

## Result

The BMI of the subject was ……… kg/m² (………) and waist circumference ……… cm (………).

## Precautions

1. Calibrate and zero the scale before use.
2. Remove shoes and heavy clothing.
3. Convert height from cm to m before calculating.
4. BMI is not suitable alone for children (age-specific charts are used), pregnant women and very muscular people.
5. Be sensitive and non-judgemental when discussing weight.

## Viva questions

1. **Formula of BMI?** Weight in kg divided by the square of height in metres.
2. **Normal BMI for Asian Indians?** 18.5–22.9 kg/m².
3. **BMI cut-off for obesity in India?** 25 kg/m² or more.
4. **Why measure waist?** To detect central obesity, linked to diabetes and heart disease.
5. **Waist cut-off for Indian men and women?** 90 cm and 80 cm.
practicals.title: BMI measurement

# Counselling a simulated patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus (with insulin pen use)

**Aim:** To counsel a simulated patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus on the disease, medicines, self-monitoring and lifestyle, and to train the patient in the use of an insulin pen.

## Principle

Type 2 diabetes is a long-term disease in which the body does not use insulin properly, causing high blood glucose. Good control prevents damage to the eyes, kidneys, nerves, heart and feet. Counselling follows the four stages – introduction, content, process and closing – and ends with teach-back so that the patient can show correct use of the pen.

## Requirements

Model community pharmacy counselling area, simulated prescription (for example metformin 500 mg twice daily and a basal insulin by pen), dummy insulin pen with pen needles, glucometer for demonstration, patient information leaflet on diabetes, structured assessment form.

## Procedure

1. **Introduction:** greet, introduce yourself, confirm identity, explain the purpose and time, ensure privacy, ask what the patient already knows.
2. **Disease:** explain in simple words what diabetes is and why lifelong control matters.
3. **Metformin:** take with or just after meals; stomach upset early usually settles; tell the doctor before X-ray dye tests or surgery.
4. **Insulin pen technique (demonstrate, then ask the patient to repeat):**
   1. Wash hands; check insulin name and expiry; roll cloudy insulin gently if required.
   2. Attach a new needle; remove both caps.
   3. Prime: dial 2 units, hold needle up, tap, press until a drop appears.
   4. Dial the prescribed dose.
   5. Clean skin if dirty; inject into the abdomen (away from the navel) or thigh at 90°.
   6. Press the button fully and hold for about 10 seconds before withdrawing.
   7. Remove and discard the needle in a hard container; replace the cap.
   8. Rotate injection sites within an area to avoid lumps.
5. **Storage:** unopened pens in a refrigerator at 2–8 °C, never frozen; the in-use pen at room temperature for the period stated on the leaflet; never share pens.
6. **Hypoglycaemia:** sweating, shaking, hunger, confusion → 15–20 g quick sugar (glucose, sugar, juice), recheck after 15 minutes; carry sugar and an identity card.
7. **Monitoring:** home glucose testing with a meter; HbA1c every 3–6 months; yearly eye, kidney and foot checks.
8. **Lifestyle:** regular meals, less sugar and refined starch, more fibre, regular exercise, weight control, no smoking, limit alcohol.
9. **Foot care:** inspect daily, wear proper footwear, treat cuts early.
10. **Closing:** summarise three key points, teach-back of pen technique, give leaflet and contact number, plan follow-up, document.

## Observations (structured assessment)

| Item | Done (✓/✗) |
| --- | --- |
| Greeted, introduced, confirmed identity, privacy | |
| Explained disease simply | |
| Metformin counselling | |
| Demonstrated insulin pen steps in order | |
| Patient performed teach-back correctly | |
| Storage of insulin explained | |
| Hypoglycaemia recognition and action | |
| Monitoring and lifestyle advice | |
| Summary, leaflet, follow-up, documentation | |

## Result

The simulated patient was counselled on type 2 diabetes and correctly demonstrated insulin pen use by teach-back.

## Precautions

1. Use simple language and the patient's own language.
2. Do not overload – focus on key points, give a leaflet for the rest.
3. Use a new needle for every injection; never share pens.
4. Check understanding by teach-back, not by asking "Do you understand?"

## Viva questions

1. **Why hold the pen for 10 seconds after injecting?** So that the full dose is delivered.
2. **Why rotate injection sites?** To prevent fatty lumps that affect absorption.
3. **Storage of unopened insulin?** 2–8 °C in a refrigerator, not frozen.
4. **First aid for hypoglycaemia?** 15–20 g quick-acting sugar, recheck in 15 minutes.
5. **What is HbA1c?** A blood test showing average glucose over about 3 months.
practicals.title: Counselling: type 2 diabetes mellitus (insulin pen)

# Counselling a simulated patient with primary hypertension

**Aim:** To counsel a simulated patient with primary (essential) hypertension on the disease, medicines, home BP monitoring and lifestyle changes.

## Principle

Primary hypertension is persistently raised blood pressure without a single identifiable cause. It usually causes no symptoms but damages the heart, brain, kidneys and eyes. Most patients need lifelong medicines plus lifestyle changes, so adherence is the key counselling goal.

## Requirements

Counselling area, simulated prescription (for example amlodipine 5 mg once daily and telmisartan 40 mg once daily), digital BP monitor for demonstration, BP diary, leaflet on hypertension, assessment form.

## Procedure

1. **Introduction:** greet, introduce, confirm identity, purpose, privacy; ask what the doctor told the patient (prime questions).
2. **Disease:** "high BP is silent but harms the heart, brain and kidneys; treatment controls it but usually does not cure it."
3. **Medicines:**
   - Take every day at the same time, even when feeling well.
   - Do not stop suddenly without the doctor's advice.
   - Amlodipine – ankle swelling, flushing, headache.
   - Telmisartan / other ARBs and ACE inhibitors – dizziness; ACE inhibitors may cause dry cough; kidney and potassium tests as advised; not in pregnancy.
   - Diuretics (if prescribed) – take in the morning.
   - Rise slowly from lying or sitting to avoid dizziness.
4. **Home BP monitoring:** demonstrate the digital monitor; rest 5 minutes, arm at heart level, two readings, record in a diary and show it to the doctor.
5. **Lifestyle:** reduce salt (avoid pickles, papad, packaged snacks); more fruits and vegetables; exercise about 30 minutes most days; weight control; stop smoking; limit alcohol; manage stress; good sleep.
6. **Avoid self-medication** with NSAIDs and decongestant cold medicines that can raise BP – ask the pharmacist first.
7. **Warning signs:** severe headache, chest pain, breathlessness, weakness of one side, blurred vision → emergency care.
8. **Closing:** summary, teach-back of how and when to take each tablet, leaflet, follow-up for BP check, documentation.

## Observations (structured assessment)

| Item | Done (✓/✗) |
| --- | --- |
| Opening and privacy | |
| Disease explained simply | |
| Dose, timing and daily use of each medicine | |
| Side effects and what to do | |
| Home BP monitoring demonstrated | |
| Lifestyle advice (salt, exercise, smoking, alcohol, weight) | |
| OTC drugs to avoid | |
| Warning signs | |
| Teach-back and follow-up | |

## Result

The simulated patient was counselled on hypertension and correctly explained the medicine schedule and home BP measurement.

## Precautions

1. Stress that feeling well is not a reason to stop.
2. Advice on salt must be practical for Indian diets.
3. Be non-judgemental about smoking and alcohol.
4. Refer very high readings or warning symptoms.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is hypertension called a silent killer?** It usually has no symptoms but causes stroke, heart and kidney damage.
2. **Common side effect of amlodipine?** Ankle swelling.
3. **Which OTC products may raise BP?** NSAIDs and decongestants.
4. **Main dietary advice?** Reduce salt; more fruit and vegetables.
5. **Why not stop beta-blockers suddenly?** Risk of rebound rise in BP and heart problems.
practicals.title: Counselling: primary hypertension

# Counselling a simulated patient with asthma (inhaler, spacer and nebulizer use)

**Aim:** To counsel a simulated patient with asthma on the disease, reliever and preventer medicines, and the correct use of a metered-dose inhaler, spacer, dry powder inhaler and nebulizer.

## Principle

Asthma is long-term inflammation of the airways with episodes of wheezing, breathlessness, chest tightness and cough. **Relievers** (short-acting β2 agonists such as salbutamol) open the airways quickly. **Preventers** (inhaled corticosteroids such as budesonide) reduce inflammation when used every day. Most treatment failures are due to poor inhaler technique and irregular preventer use, so the pharmacist checks technique at every visit.

## Requirements

Placebo metered-dose inhaler (MDI), spacer with mouthpiece and face mask, dummy dry powder inhaler (DPI), nebulizer with mask, peak flow meter, asthma action plan format, leaflet, assessment form.

## Procedure

1. **Introduction** and prime questions.
2. **Disease and triggers:** dust, smoke, pollen, pets, cold air, infections, exercise; avoid triggers and smoking.
3. **Reliever vs preventer:** reliever for symptoms; preventer daily even when well; needing the reliever more than usual means asthma is not controlled.
4. **MDI technique (demonstrate, then teach-back):**
   1. Remove cap, shake well.
   2. Sit or stand upright; breathe out fully away from the inhaler.
   3. Seal lips around the mouthpiece.
   4. Start a slow deep breath in and press the canister once.
   5. Continue breathing in slowly and deeply.
   6. Hold breath for about 10 seconds or as long as comfortable.
   7. Wait about 30–60 seconds before a second puff.
   8. After a steroid inhaler, rinse mouth with water and spit.
5. **Spacer:** fit inhaler, shake, one puff into the spacer, breathe in slowly and deeply (or 4–5 normal breaths through the mask for small children); clean the spacer as instructed and let it air-dry.
6. **DPI:** load the dose; do not shake; breathe out away from the device; breathe in **quickly and deeply**; hold the breath; never breathe into the device; keep it dry.
7. **Nebulizer:** put the measured solution into the cup, attach mask or mouthpiece, sit upright, breathe normally until the mist stops (about 10 minutes), wash and dry the parts after use.
8. **Monitoring:** peak flow diary; explain green, yellow and red zones of the action plan.
9. **Emergency:** reliever not helping, cannot speak in full sentences, lips turning blue → emergency care.
10. **Closing:** summary, teach-back, leaflet, follow-up, documentation.

## Observations (structured assessment)

| Device step checked | Patient correct (✓/✗) |
| --- | --- |
| Shakes MDI | |
| Breathes out before use | |
| Coordinates press with slow breath in | |
| Holds breath about 10 s | |
| Rinses mouth after steroid | |
| Uses spacer correctly | |
| DPI: fast deep breath, does not shake | |
| Nebulizer set-up and cleaning | |
| Knows reliever vs preventer | |

## Result

The simulated patient was counselled on asthma and demonstrated correct inhaler and spacer technique by teach-back.

## Precautions

1. Always demonstrate with a placebo device, then watch the patient.
2. Do not shake DPIs or breathe into them.
3. Stress daily use of preventers.
4. Refer patients with poor control or frequent reliever use.

## Viva questions

1. **Why rinse the mouth after an inhaled steroid?** To prevent oral thrush and hoarseness.
2. **Advantage of a spacer?** Less coordination needed, more drug reaches the lungs, less in the mouth.
3. **How is breathing different for a DPI?** A quick, deep breath in.
4. **Example of a reliever?** Salbutamol.
5. **Sign of poor asthma control?** Needing the reliever often.

# Counselling a simulated patient with hyperlipidaemia

**Aim:** To counsel a simulated patient with hyperlipidaemia on the condition, lipid-lowering medicines and diet and lifestyle changes.

## Principle

Hyperlipidaemia is raised blood fats (cholesterol and/or triglycerides). High LDL ("bad") cholesterol and low HDL ("good") cholesterol increase the risk of heart attack and stroke. It causes no symptoms, so patients often stop treatment. **Statins** (atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, simvastatin) lower LDL cholesterol and reduce cardiovascular risk. Lifestyle change is part of every treatment plan.

## Requirements

Counselling area, simulated prescription (for example atorvastatin 10 mg once daily), sample lipid report, food chart, leaflet, assessment form.

## Procedure

1. **Introduction** and prime questions.
2. **Condition:** explain cholesterol, LDL and HDL in simple words; it is silent but blocks arteries over years.
3. **Explain the lipid report:**

| Test | Desirable (adults) |
| --- | --- |
| Total cholesterol | Below 200 mg/dL |
| Triglycerides | Below 150 mg/dL |
| HDL cholesterol | 40 mg/dL or more (men), 50 mg/dL or more (women) |
| LDL cholesterol | Target set by the doctor according to the patient's risk |

4. **Statin counselling:**
   - Take once daily, every day; atorvastatin and rosuvastatin at any fixed time; simvastatin is usually taken in the evening.
   - Report unexplained muscle pain, weakness or dark urine.
   - Liver tests as advised.
   - Not to be used in pregnancy or breast-feeding.
   - Avoid large amounts of grapefruit juice with simvastatin and atorvastatin; limit alcohol.
   - Continue long term; benefit is in preventing heart attack, not in feeling better.
5. **Diet:** less saturated fat (ghee, butter, fried and fast foods), avoid trans fats (vanaspati, bakery items), more fibre (whole grains, oats, pulses, fruits, vegetables), use small amounts of healthy oils, control sugar and refined carbohydrates (raise triglycerides).
6. **Lifestyle:** regular exercise, weight control, stop smoking, limit alcohol, control BP and diabetes.
7. **Follow-up:** repeat lipid test as advised.
8. **Closing:** summary, teach-back, leaflet, documentation.

## Observations (structured assessment)

| Item | Done (✓/✗) |
| --- | --- |
| Condition explained | |
| Lipid report explained | |
| Statin dose and timing | |
| Muscle pain warning | |
| Pregnancy and interactions | |
| Diet advice | |
| Exercise and smoking advice | |
| Teach-back and follow-up | |

## Result

The simulated patient was counselled on hyperlipidaemia, statin use and lifestyle changes.

## Precautions

1. Give practical Indian diet examples.
2. Stress long-term adherence even without symptoms.
3. Refer muscle pain or yellowing of eyes promptly.

## Viva questions

1. **Which cholesterol is called "good"?** HDL.
2. **Main side effect to report with statins?** Unexplained muscle pain or weakness.
3. **Why is simvastatin given in the evening?** Cholesterol production is higher at night and it acts for a short time.
4. **Can statins be used in pregnancy?** No.
5. **Name two foods rich in trans fats.** Vanaspati and many bakery and fried snack items.

# Counselling a simulated patient with rheumatoid arthritis

**Aim:** To counsel a simulated patient with rheumatoid arthritis on the disease, disease-modifying and pain medicines, monitoring and joint care.

## Principle

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a long-term autoimmune disease in which the body's immune system attacks the lining of joints, causing pain, swelling and morning stiffness, usually in small joints of the hands and feet on both sides. Early and regular use of **disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs)** such as methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine and sulfasalazine slows joint damage. NSAIDs and short courses of corticosteroids relieve symptoms.

## Requirements

Counselling area, simulated prescription (for example methotrexate tablets once weekly, folic acid, and an NSAID as needed), weekly calendar, leaflet, assessment form.

## Procedure

1. **Introduction** and prime questions.
2. **Disease:** long-term; medicines control it and protect joints; benefit of DMARDs takes weeks to months.
3. **Methotrexate (most important safety point):**
   - Taken **once a week**, on the same day each week – never daily. Mark the day on a calendar.
   - Folic acid is given to reduce side effects, on the day(s) the doctor states.
   - Regular blood tests (blood counts, liver and kidney function).
   - Avoid alcohol.
   - Report mouth ulcers, sore throat, fever, unusual bruising, breathlessness or cough.
   - Avoid pregnancy during treatment and for the time the doctor advises afterwards (both men and women should ask).
   - Check with the pharmacist before taking other medicines (some antibiotics such as trimethoprim interact).
4. **Hydroxychloroquine (if prescribed):** take with food; regular eye check-ups.
5. **NSAIDs:** take with food; report stomach pain or black stools.
6. **Corticosteroids (if prescribed):** take in the morning with food; do not stop suddenly after long use.
7. **Joint care:** balance rest and gentle exercise; physiotherapy; warm compresses for stiffness; joint protection (use both hands, avoid tight gripping); healthy weight; stop smoking.
8. **Vaccination:** discuss vaccines with the doctor because some DMARDs lower immunity.
9. **Closing:** summary, teach-back ("Which day will you take methotrexate?"), leaflet, follow-up, documentation.

## Observations (structured assessment)

| Item | Done (✓/✗) |
| --- | --- |
| Disease explained | |
| Methotrexate once weekly – patient repeats the day correctly | |
| Folic acid timing | |
| Blood test monitoring | |
| Danger symptoms to report | |
| Pregnancy, alcohol, interactions | |
| NSAID and steroid advice | |
| Joint care and exercise | |
| Teach-back and follow-up | |

## Result

The simulated patient was counselled on rheumatoid arthritis and correctly stated the once-weekly methotrexate schedule.

## Precautions

1. Repeat and confirm "once a week" for methotrexate – daily dosing has caused serious harm.
2. Use a calendar or weekly reminder.
3. Refer fever, mouth ulcers or bruising promptly.

## Viva questions

1. **How often is methotrexate taken for RA?** Once a week.
2. **Why is folic acid given?** To reduce methotrexate side effects.
3. **Which tests are needed with methotrexate?** Blood counts and liver and kidney function.
4. **What is a DMARD?** A drug that slows the disease process and joint damage.
5. **Eye check-ups are needed with which drug?** Hydroxychloroquine.

# Counselling simulated patients for minor ailments

**Aim:** To respond to symptoms and counsel simulated patients for minor ailments (any three of: headache, GI disturbances – nausea, vomiting, dyspepsia, diarrhoea, constipation – worm infestations, pyrexia, upper respiratory tract infections, skin infections, oral and dental disorders).

## Principle

When a person asks for help with a symptom, the pharmacist gathers information in a structured way (**WWHAM** or **ASMETHOD**), looks for danger signs, and decides whether to give self-care advice, supply a suitable OTC product, or refer to a doctor. Every consultation ends with a **safety net** – telling the patient when to come back or see a doctor.

## Requirements

Model pharmacy counter and counselling area, scenario cards, OTC products and dummy packs, thermometer, reference book, leaflets, structured assessment form.

## Procedure (common to every scenario)

1. Greet the patient and move to a private area if needed.
2. Ask WWHAM: Who is it for? What are the symptoms? How long? Action already taken? Medicines already taken?
3. Ask about danger symptoms for that ailment (table below).
4. Decide: self-care only / OTC + advice / refer.
5. If supplying, choose a product suitable for age, pregnancy and other diseases and medicines.
6. Counsel: dose, how and when to take, duration, side effects, what to avoid.
7. Give self-care advice.
8. Safety net: "If not better in … days, or if … happens, see a doctor."
9. Check understanding (teach-back) and record.

## Scenario guide

| Ailment | Key questions | Self-care and OTC | Refer if |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Headache | Type, site, duration, triggers, vision, fever, injury | Rest, fluids, regular meals and sleep; paracetamol (or ibuprofen with food) | Sudden severe, with fever and stiff neck, after head injury, with weakness or vision loss, frequent use of painkillers |
| Nausea and vomiting | Duration, blood, pain, pregnancy, drugs, travel | ORS sips, small bland meals; antihistamine before travel for motion sickness | Blood, more than 24–48 h, dehydration, severe pain, pregnancy, diabetes |
| Dyspepsia (indigestion) | Relation to food, age, weight loss, black stools, NSAID use | Small meals, avoid spicy fatty food and late meals, stop smoking; antacid | Age over about 50 with new symptoms, weight loss, difficulty swallowing, black stools, vomiting blood |
| Diarrhoea | Frequency, blood, fever, dehydration, age | ORS, continue feeding; zinc for children; loperamide only for adults without fever or blood | Blood, fever, dehydration, more than 2–3 days (24 h in infants) |
| Constipation | Usual habit, diet, drugs, blood, weight loss | Fibre, fluids, exercise; ispaghula, lactulose | Blood, weight loss, change of habit after middle age, more than 2 weeks |
| Worm infestation | Itching around anus at night (threadworm), worms seen, family | Albendazole as per label for age; hygiene – hand washing, short nails, washing bedding; treat family members as advised | Children under the label's minimum age, pregnancy, weight loss, persistent symptoms |
| Pyrexia (fever) | Temperature, duration, rash, travel, other symptoms | Fluids, rest, tepid sponging; paracetamol by dose and weight; no aspirin in children | More than 3 days, infants under 3 months, fits, non-fading rash, stiff neck, breathing difficulty |
| URTI (cold, sore throat, cough) | Symptoms, duration, fever, breathlessness, asthma | Fluids, steam, saline drops, salt gargles, lozenges, antihistamine, paracetamol; no antibiotics | Cough more than 2–3 weeks, blood in sputum, breathlessness, high fever, ear pain |
| Skin infection | Appearance, site, itch, spread, diabetes | Fungal – clotrimazole cream; scabies – permethrin 5% for whole family; minor cuts – clean and antiseptic | Spreading redness, pus, fever, scalp or nail involvement, diabetic patient |
| Oral and dental | Ulcer duration, tooth pain, swelling, tobacco use | Mouth ulcer – choline salicylate gel, salt rinse; toothache – painkiller and dentist; gum bleeding – brushing, flossing, chlorhexidine | Ulcer more than 3 weeks, facial swelling, fever; all toothache to a dentist |

## Observations (structured assessment for each scenario)

| Item | Scenario 1 | Scenario 2 | Scenario 3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| WWHAM / ASMETHOD used | | | |
| Danger symptoms asked | | | |
| Correct decision (advise / OTC / refer) | | | |
| Suitable product and dose | | | |
| Self-care advice | | | |
| Safety-net advice | | | |
| Teach-back and record | | | |

## Result

Three simulated patients with minor ailments (………, ………, ………) were assessed and counselled, with referral where needed.

## Precautions

1. Never supply prescription-only drugs (antibiotics, steroids, strong antiemetics) without a prescription.
2. Check age limits and pregnancy on product labels.
3. Always give red-flag and safety-net advice.
4. Respect privacy for embarrassing symptoms (worms, piles, skin).

## Viva questions

1. **Expand WWHAM.** Who, What symptoms, How long, Action taken, Medicines.
2. **First-line treatment of diarrhoea?** ORS.
3. **Why treat the whole family for threadworm or scabies?** To prevent reinfection.
4. **When should a headache be referred urgently?** Sudden severe headache, or with fever and stiff neck, weakness or after injury.
5. **Should antibiotics be given for a common cold?** No – it is viral.

# Handling dummy dosage forms with correct administration techniques

**Aim:** To demonstrate and teach the correct handling and administration of common dosage forms using dummy products: oral liquids with measuring cup, cap or dropper, eye drops, inhalers, nasal drops, insulin pen, nebulizers, different types of tablets, transdermal patches, enemas and suppositories.

## Principle

A correct medicine can fail if it is used wrongly. The pharmacist demonstrates each technique with a dummy product and then asks the patient to repeat it (**teach-back**), correcting any mistakes.

## Requirements

Dummy products: oral liquid with measuring cup, dosing cap, oral syringe and dropper; eye drops; nasal drops and spray; placebo inhaler and spacer; insulin pen; nebulizer; plain, enteric-coated, sustained-release, sublingual, chewable, dispersible and effervescent tablets; transdermal patch; enema pack; suppository. Water, tissues, gloves, assessment form.

## Procedure

| Dosage form | Steps to teach |
| --- | --- |
| Oral liquids | Shake if suspension; use the cup, cap, oral syringe or dropper supplied (not a kitchen spoon); read the measure at eye level on a flat surface; for babies, give slowly into the side of the cheek with an oral syringe; wash the measure after use |
| Plain tablets / capsules | Swallow with a full glass of water, sitting or standing |
| Enteric-coated and sustained-release tablets | Swallow whole; do not crush or chew |
| Sublingual tablet (e.g. glyceryl trinitrate) | Place under the tongue, let it dissolve; do not swallow; sit down |
| Chewable tablet | Chew fully before swallowing |
| Dispersible / effervescent tablet | Dissolve in the stated amount of water and drink at once |
| Eye drops | Wash hands; tilt head back; pull lower lid; one drop into the pocket without touching the tip; close eye, press the inner corner for about a minute; 5 minutes between different drops |
| Nasal drops | Blow nose; tilt head back (or lie with head over the bed edge); instil drops; stay in position a minute; clean dropper |
| Nasal spray | Blow nose; head slightly forward; insert tip, aim away from the middle of the nose; spray while breathing in gently |
| Inhaler and spacer | Shake, breathe out, seal lips, press and breathe in slowly, hold 10 seconds; rinse mouth after steroid (see asthma counselling guide) |
| Insulin pen | New needle, prime 2 units, dial dose, inject at 90°, hold 10 seconds, rotate sites (see diabetes counselling guide) |
| Nebulizer | Measure solution into the cup, attach mask, sit upright, breathe normally until the mist stops, clean parts |
| Transdermal patch | Clean, dry, hairless skin; peel liner without touching the adhesive; press for 30 seconds; change at the stated interval; rotate sites; fold used patch sticky sides together before disposal |
| Rectal suppository | Wash hands; remove wrapper; moisten tip with water; lie on the left side with upper knee bent; insert pointed end first about 2–3 cm beyond the anal sphincter; stay lying a few minutes |
| Enema | Lie on the left side with knees bent; lubricate nozzle; insert gently; squeeze the pack slowly; withdraw; hold the liquid for the time on the label |

1. Explain the purpose of the dosage form.
2. Demonstrate each step with the dummy product.
3. Ask the patient (classmate) to repeat the steps.
4. Correct errors and repeat until right.
5. Give storage advice (eye drops discarded after the in-use period, suppositories in a cool place, insulin in a refrigerator).
6. Record on the assessment form.

## Observations

| Dosage form | Demonstrated (✓) | Teach-back correct (✓/✗) | Errors corrected |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Oral liquid with oral syringe | | | |
| Eye drops | | | |
| Inhaler | | | |
| Suppository | | | |
| (others) | | | |

## Result

Correct administration techniques for the listed dosage forms were demonstrated and checked by teach-back.

## Precautions

1. Use dummy or placebo products only; never use real medicines on classmates.
2. Maintain hygiene – wash hands; do not touch dropper or nozzle tips.
3. Use the measuring device provided with the medicine.
4. Respect privacy when explaining rectal products.

## Viva questions

1. **Why not use a kitchen spoon?** Sizes vary, giving a wrong dose.
2. **Why press the inner corner of the eye after eye drops?** Reduces drainage into the nose and body, keeping more drug in the eye.
3. **Why must sustained-release tablets not be crushed?** The whole dose would be released at once.
4. **How is a sublingual tablet used?** Placed under the tongue to dissolve.
5. **Which side should a patient lie on for an enema or suppository?** The left side, with the upper knee bent.
practicals.title: Handling dummy dosage forms and administration techniques

# Use of community pharmacy software and digital health tools

**Aim:** To use community pharmacy software for billing, inventory and records, and to become familiar with digital health tools useful in community practice.

## Principle

Pharmacy management software keeps sales, purchases, stock, expiry, accounts and patient records in one computer system. It reduces errors, saves time and gives reports that help in management. Digital health tools – e-prescriptions, health record apps, reminder apps, teleconsultation platforms and connected devices – extend the pharmacist's services beyond the counter.

## Requirements

Computer with community pharmacy software (demo or trial version), barcode scanner and label printer if available, dummy invoices and prescriptions, smartphone with a medication reminder app, practical record book.

## Procedure

### A. Pharmacy software

1. **Master data:** create item records (name, generic name, strength, pack, manufacturer, HSN code, GST rate, schedule, storage condition, reorder level) and supplier records.
2. **Purchase entry:** enter a dummy invoice with batch numbers, expiry dates, quantity, rate and MRP; check that stock increases.
3. **Billing:** prepare a sale bill for a simulated prescription; note how the software selects the batch with the earliest expiry (FEFO) and blocks expired batches.
4. **Scheduled drugs:** bill a Schedule H1 item and view the automatic H1 register entry with patient and prescriber details.
5. **Patient record:** create a patient profile with allergies and long-term medicines; check any interaction alert.
6. **Reports:** print stock, reorder, near-expiry, sales by date and supplier dues reports.
7. **Accounts:** view day book, cash book and GST summary prepared by the software.
8. **Backup:** take a data backup and note the method.

### B. Digital health tools

1. Set a medication reminder for a simulated patient in a reminder app.
2. Study how an e-prescription or teleconsultation prescription is presented and verified.
3. Note how health records can be linked under the national digital health mission (ABHA health ID) – study only, using demonstration material; do not enter real personal data.
4. Use a connected glucometer or BP app if available to record and share readings.
5. List privacy and data-security precautions.

## Observations

| Task | Completed (✓) | Remarks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Item and supplier master created | | |
| Purchase invoice entered | | |
| Sale bill with FEFO batch | | |
| H1 register entry created | | |
| Interaction alert checked | | |
| Reorder / expiry report printed | | |
| Backup taken | | |
| Reminder app set | | |

Features of the software studied:

| Feature | Present (Yes/No) |
| --- | --- |
| GST billing | |
| Batch and expiry tracking | |
| Reorder alerts | |
| Interaction checking | |
| Patient medication records | |
| SMS / app reminders | |
| Cloud backup | |

## Result

Billing, purchase entry, inventory reports and scheduled-drug records were carried out using pharmacy software, and selected digital health tools were studied.

## Precautions

1. Use dummy data only; never enter real patient information in a demo system.
2. Keep passwords private; log out after use.
3. Take regular backups.
4. Check software output (bill, label) before giving it to the patient.

## Viva questions

1. **Two advantages of pharmacy software?** Fast accurate billing; automatic expiry and reorder alerts.
2. **How does software help with Schedule H1?** It creates the register entry automatically.
3. **What is FEFO?** First expiry, first out.
4. **What is ABHA?** Ayushman Bharat Health Account – a digital health ID under ABDM.
5. **Why is data backup important?** To prevent loss of records if the computer fails.

# Field visit to a community pharmacy and a medicine distributor

**Aim:** To visit a community pharmacy and a medicine distributor, observe the professional activities of community pharmacists and the supply chain, and write an individual report.

## Principle

The ER-2020 practical syllabus includes a group field visit so that students see real practice: how a licensed pharmacy is organised, how prescriptions are handled, how stock reaches the pharmacy from manufacturers through distributors, and how records and licences are maintained.

## Requirements

Permission letters from the college, visit checklist, notebook, college identity card. Photographs only with the owner's permission and never of patients or prescriptions.

## Procedure

1. Before the visit, revise licences (Form 20, 21, 20B, 21B), schedules (H, H1, X), storage conditions and inventory terms.
2. At the **community pharmacy**, observe and note:
   - display of licences and pharmacist registration certificate;
   - layout – dispensing counter, counselling area, refrigerator, Schedule X cupboard, expired-goods area;
   - prescription receiving, checking, billing and labelling;
   - patient counselling and OTC requests (without listening to private details);
   - registers (H1, Schedule X), temperature log, purchase and sales records;
   - software used and stock arrangement;
   - services offered (BP, glucose, home delivery).
3. At the **distributor / wholesaler**, observe:
   - wholesale licence and storage areas;
   - receipt of goods from manufacturers, checking of batch and expiry;
   - cold-chain storage (cold room or refrigerators, ice packs and boxes for dispatch);
   - order processing, picking, invoicing and delivery to retailers;
   - handling of returns and expired goods.
4. Ask the pharmacist and distributor about common challenges (shortages, expiry losses, regulations).
5. After the visit, write an individual report.

## Observations (report format)

```text
1. Date, names and addresses of places visited
2. Licences and registrations seen
3. Layout of the pharmacy (simple sketch)
4. Dispensing process observed
5. Records and registers maintained
6. Storage and cold-chain arrangements
7. Supply chain: manufacturer → C&F agent → distributor/wholesaler → retailer → patient
8. Services offered to patients
9. Problems discussed
10. What I learnt and suggestions
```

## Result

A field visit to a community pharmacy and a medicine distributor was completed, and an individual report on pharmacy practice and the supply chain was submitted.

## Precautions

1. Behave professionally; follow the instructions of the host.
2. Do not disturb patients or record confidential information.
3. Do not touch stock or records without permission.

## Viva questions

1. **Which licences would you expect at a retail pharmacy?** Form 20 and Form 21 (and Schedule X licence if stocked).
2. **Name the stages of the medicine supply chain.** Manufacturer, C&F agent, distributor or wholesaler, retailer, patient.
3. **What is a cold chain?** Keeping temperature-sensitive products at the required temperature (often 2–8 °C) from manufacture to use.
4. **Which register is required for Schedule H1 drugs?** A separate H1 register kept for 3 years.
5. **Who issues the wholesale drug licence?** The State Licensing Authority.
